chapter: Vascular Syndromes of the Forebrain, Brainstem, and
section: Anterior vs Middle Cerebral Artery Syndromes
source_quote: Involvement of hemispheric ACA branches often results in contralateral weakness mainly involving the leg. There may be lack of initiative or abulia.
vignette: A 74-year-old man presents with acute weakness of the left lower extremity that is far more severe than the left upper extremity (leg strength 1/5, arm strength 4/5, face strength normal). He has marked left leg sensory loss to pinprick and vibration, urinary incontinence, and exhibits profound abulia with delayed verbal responses and bilateral grasping reflexes.
question: Which arterial territory is occluded?
options: Right middle cerebral artery (MCA) superior division
Right anterior cerebral artery (ACA)
Right middle cerebral artery (MCA) inferior division
Right posterior cerebral artery (PCA)
Right anterior choroidal artery

explanation.why_correct: The anterior cerebral artery (ACA) supplies the medial surface of the cerebral hemisphere, which corresponds to the homunculus representation of the contralateral lower extremity (paracentral lobule). Consequently, ACA infarction produces contralateral hemiparesis and hemisensory loss affecting the LEG far more than the arm, while completely sparing the face. Involvement of the medial frontal lobe, cingulate gyrus, and supplementary motor area accounts for the abulia, urinary urgency/incontinence, and primitive grasp reflexes.
distractors: MCA superior division infarction causes hemiparesis affecting the face and ARM far more than the leg (brachiofacial), with Broca aphasia (left) or hemineglect (right).
MCA inferior division infarction causes homonymous hemianopia and sensory loss, sparing motor power.
PCA infarction causes homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing and thalamic sensory loss, not isolated leg paresis.
Anterior choroidal artery infarction causes dense, equal hemiplegia of the face, arm, and leg (posterior limb of internal capsule) with hemianesthesia.
explanation.key_point: Anterior cerebral artery (ACA) infarction produces leg > arm weakness and sensory loss, accompanied by abulia, urinary incontinence, and primitive frontal release reflexes.

chapter: Vascular Syndromes of the Forebrain, Brainstem, and
vignette: A 79-year-old woman develops profound hypotension during emergency coronary bypass surgery. Postoperatively, when she awakens, she has severe bilateral proximal arm and leg weakness ('man-in-a-barrel' syndrome), such that she cannot raise her arms or thighs, but has preserved movement in her hands and feet. Sensory testing shows patchy bilateral proximal trunk numbness. Cranial nerves, language, and facial movements are normal.
question: What is the hemodynamic mechanism and localization of 'man-in-a-barrel' syndrome?
options: Bilateral cortical borderzone (watershed) infarctions between the anterior and middle cerebral arteries
Bilateral anterior spinal artery infarction in the mid-cervical cord
Basilar artery trunk thrombosis causing locked-in syndrome
Acute bilateral brachial plexopathy from surgical positioning
Central pontine myelinolysis

explanation.why_correct: The cortical watershed (borderzone) between the anterior cerebral artery (ACA) and middle cerebral artery (MCA) territories lies in the parasagittal frontal cortex, which corresponds anatomically to the motor homunculus representation of the shoulder and hip girdles. Severe systemic hypotension selectively deprives these distal borderzones of perfusion, producing bilateral infarctions that present as proximal arm and proximal leg paralysis with distal hand and foot preservation ('man-in-a-barrel' syndrome).
distractors: Anterior spinal artery cervical cord infarction causes spastic paraplegia of both legs and flaccid arms, with bilateral loss of pain and temperature below the neck.
Basilar artery thrombosis causes quadriplegia with preserved vertical eye movements and consciousness (locked-in syndrome), not isolated proximal weakness.
Brachial plexopathy impairs the upper extremities only and causes sensory loss along peripheral distributions, sparing the lower extremities.
Central pontine myelinolysis causes pseudobulbar palsy and spastic quadriplegia, not selective proximal 'man-in-a-barrel' weakness.
explanation.key_point: Bilateral ACA-MCA watershed (borderzone) infarctions from systemic hypotension cause 'man-in-a-barrel' syndrome (bilateral proximal arm and shoulder weakness with distal sparing).

chapter: Vascular Syndromes
vignette: A 71-year-old woman develops acute weakness and sensory loss. Neurological examination reveals severe spastic paresis and dense loss of pinprick and proprioception in her right lower extremity, while strength and sensation in her right face and upper extremity are almost completely preserved. She is remarkably indifferent, responds with long latencies (abulia), and has uninhibited urinary incontinence.
question: Which vascular territory is infarcted in this patient?
options: Left anterior cerebral artery (ACA) distal to the anterior communicating artery
Left middle cerebral artery (MCA) superior division
Left anterior choroidal artery
Left posterior cerebral artery calcarine branch
Left lenticulostriate penetrating arteries

explanation.why_correct: The anterior cerebral artery (ACA) supplies the medial surface of the cerebral hemisphere, including the paracentral lobule (which contains the motor and sensory representations of the contralateral lower extremity and foot). ACA infarction classically causes contralateral motor and sensory deficits affecting the LEG disproportionately more than the arm or face (the reverse of MCA strokes). In addition, ischemia to the medial frontal lobe, supplementary motor area, and cingulate cortex results in abulia (psychomotor slowing, apathy) and frontal lobe incontinence due to loss of the medial frontal micturition inhibition center.
distractors: MCA superior division stroke affects the convexity of the motor strip, causing weakness of the face and arm much more than the leg, with Broca aphasia.
Anterior choroidal stroke affects the posterior limb of internal capsule, causing dense, proportional hemiplegia (face = arm = leg) with hemianopia.
PCA calcarine stroke causes contralateral homonymous hemianopia without primary leg motor paresis.
Lenticulostriate stroke in the posterior limb causes pure motor hemiparesis equally affecting face, arm, and leg.
explanation.key_point: ACA infarction causes contralateral lower extremity motor and sensory loss exceeding arm/face deficits, associated with abulia and frontal urinary incontinence.

chapter: Vascular Syndromes
vignette: A 56-year-old diabetic man presents with an acute stroke. Neurological exam reveals dense contralateral right hemiplegia equally involving the face, arm, and leg; contralateral right hemianesthesia for all modalities; and a complete right homonymous hemianopia. Higher cognitive functions including language, praxias, and neglect are completely intact.
question: What classic triad is produced by infarction of the anterior choroidal artery (AChA)?
options: Ipsilateral cranial nerve III palsy, contralateral ataxia, and chorea
Contralateral hemiplegia (posterior limb of internal capsule), hemianesthesia (thalamocortical fibers), and homonymous hemianopia (retrolenticular capsule / optic tract / lateral geniculate body)
Contralateral leg weakness, abulia, and grasping reflex
Receptive aphasia, visual agnosia, and prosopagnosia
Ophthalmoplegia, cerebellar ataxia, and areflexia

explanation.why_correct: The anterior choroidal artery (AChA) arises from the internal carotid artery and supplies critical deep structures: (1) Posterior limb of the internal capsule (corticospinal fibers -> contralateral dense hemiplegia); (2) Posterior thalamocortical sensory radiations / retrolenticular internal capsule (somatosensory fibers -> contralateral hemianesthesia); (3) Retrolenticular internal capsule, optic tract, and lateral geniculate nucleus (visual fibers -> contralateral homonymous hemianopia). The classic AChA triad is contralateral hemiplegia, hemianesthesia, and homonymous hemianopia, with notable preservation of cortical higher functions (no aphasia or neglect).
distractors: CN III palsy with contralateral ataxia/tremor defines midbrain syndromes (Claude/Benedikt syndrome), supplied by PCA/basilar perforators.
Contralateral leg weakness and abulia characterize the ACA territory.
Wernicke aphasia and agnosias characterize the MCA inferior division or cortical temporal strokes.
Ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and areflexia define Miller Fisher syndrome.
explanation.key_point: The anterior choroidal artery triad comprises contralateral hemiplegia, hemianesthesia, and homonymous hemianopia with preserved cortical cognitive functions.

chapter: Vascular Syndromes
vignette: A 68-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation develops an acute left posterior cerebral artery (PCA) infarction involving the calcarine cortex. Automated visual field testing reveals a complete right homonymous hemianopia, but the central 5 degrees of the visual field in both eyes are completely intact and preserved ('macular sparing').
question: What is the anatomical and vascular basis of macular sparing in PCA occipital lobe infarctions?
options: Direct innervation of the macula by the anterior ciliary arteries
Bilateral retinal ganglion cell projections from the central fovea to both lateral geniculate nuclei
Dual collateral vascular supply to the occipital pole from terminal cortical branches of the middle cerebral artery (MCA)
Sprouting of new collateral axons from the superior colliculus to the occipital pole
Macular visual fibers bypass the striate cortex and terminate in the frontal eye fields

explanation.why_correct: The primary visual cortex (Brodmann area 17) along the calcarine fissure is supplied primarily by the calcarine branch of the posterior cerebral artery (PCA). However, the representation of the macula (central 5-10 degrees of vision) occupies a disproportionately massive territory at the most posterior tip of the occipital pole. This occipital pole has a rich dual/overlapping collateral blood supply, receiving anastomotic branches from both the terminal cortical branches of the middle cerebral artery (MCA) and the PCA. Therefore, when the main PCA trunk is occluded, the MCA collaterals maintain perfusion of the occipital pole, preserving central visual acuity and central visual fields (macular sparing).
distractors: Anterior ciliary arteries supply the anterior uvea and ciliary body of the eye, not the occipital cerebral cortex.
Foveal ganglion cells split at the vertical meridian and project strictly hemispherically (contralaterally), not bilaterally to both LGNs.
Axonal sprouting takes weeks-months and cannot explain immediate macular sparing at acute stroke onset.
Macular visual fibers do not bypass the striate cortex; primary vision requires V1.
explanation.key_point: Macular sparing in PCA strokes occurs because the occipital pole receives dual collateral circulation from terminal branches of the middle cerebral artery (MCA).

chapter: Vascular Syndromes
vignette: A 63-year-old man experiences prolonged systemic hypotension and cardiac arrest during an elective procedure. Following resuscitation, neurological examination reveals severe weakness of both proximal shoulder girdles and hips (inability to lift arms above head or stand without assistance), while strength in his hands and feet is remarkably preserved ('man-in-a-barrel' syndrome).
question: Which borderzone vascular territory is damaged bilaterally to produce the 'man-in-a-barrel' syndrome?
options: Posterior cortical borderzone between the middle cerebral artery (MCA) and posterior cerebral artery (PCA)
Internal borderzone between the lenticulostriate and middle cerebral artery branches
Anterior cortical borderzone between the anterior cerebral artery (ACA) and middle cerebral artery (MCA) territories
Vertebrobasilar junction borderzone
Spinal anterior cord watershed at T1-T2

explanation.why_correct: The cortical motor strip is somatotopically organized as a homunculus: the trunk and proximal limbs (shoulder and hip) lie in the superior convexity of the cerebral cortex, right at the boundary/watershed zone between the distal perfusion territories of the anterior cerebral artery (ACA) and middle cerebral artery (MCA). During episodes of severe systemic hypotension, hypovolemia, or cardiac arrest, perfusion pressure drops lowest at these furthest distal arterial boundary zones. Bilateral ACA-MCA watershed infarctions selectively damage the cortical representations of the shoulder and hip girdles while sparing the distal hand (lateral MCA convexity) and foot (deep medial ACA), creating the classic 'man-in-a-barrel' syndrome.
distractors: MCA-PCA posterior watershed infarctions produce transcortical sensory aphasia, Balint syndrome, or cortical visual processing deficits, not proximal motor weakness.
Internal borderzone infarctions produce rosary-like subcortical white matter infarctions, often causing hemiparesis or pure motor deficits.
Vertebrobasilar borderzone ischemia produces brainstem and cerebellar symptoms.
T1-T2 spinal watershed causes paraplegia of the legs, not isolated proximal arm and hip weakness.
explanation.key_point: Bilateral ACA-MCA anterior borderzone (watershed) infarctions produce 'man-in-a-barrel' syndrome: severe proximal shoulder and hip weakness with preserved distal extremities.

chapter: Vascular Syndromes
section: Basilar Artery Occlusion / Top of the Basilar
vignette: A 69-year-old man experiences sudden stupor. When aroused, he has bilateral pupillary asymmetry, limitation of upward gaze, bilateral ptosis, and vivid visual hallucinations of colorful flowers and animals in his room (peduncular hallucinosis). Brain MRI reveals acute ischemic lesions in the rostral mesencephalon, bilateral paramedian thalami, and bilateral occipital lobes.
question: What vascular syndrome, described by C. Miller Fisher, results from embolic occlusion of the rostral termination of the basilar artery?
options: Locked-in syndrome
'Top of the basilar' syndrome
Lateral medullary syndrome
Subclavian steal syndrome
Moyamoya syndrome

explanation.why_correct: 'Top of the basilar' syndrome, classically described by C. Miller Fisher, occurs when a cardiac or vertebrobasilar embolus lodges at the bifurcation of the basilar artery into the posterior cerebral arteries (PCAs) and superior cerebellar arteries (SCAs). Ischemia affects the rostral brainstem (midbrain tegmentum), diencephalon (thalami), and occipital/temporal lobes. The syndrome is characterized by: (1) Visual deficits (cortical blindness, hemianopia, Balint syndrome); (2) Ocular motor abnormalities (vertical gaze palsy, skew deviation, pupillary abnormalities, third nerve palsies); (3) Behavioral/consciousness disturbances (fluctuating stupor, akinetic mutism, amnesia); and (4) Peduncular hallucinosis (vivid, colorful, well-formed visual hallucinations).
distractors: Locked-in syndrome is caused by ventral pontine basilar occlusion (infarction of bilateral corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts), sparing consciousness and vertical eye movements.
Lateral medullary syndrome (Wallenberg) is caused by PICA/vertebral occlusion, involving lower cranial nerves and cerebellar ataxia.
Subclavian steal syndrome causes arm claudication and transient posterior circulation hypoperfusion during arm exercise.
Moyamoya syndrome is chronic progressive stenosis of the terminal internal carotid arteries with basal collateral networks.
explanation.key_point: 'Top of the basilar' syndrome results from embolic occlusion of the rostral basilar apex, causing midbrain, thalamic, and occipital infarctions with vertical gaze palsies, coma/stupor, and peduncular hallucinosis.

chapter: Vascular Syndromes
source_quote: DCHS is the result of a lacune involving the anterior limb or genu of the internal capsule or the depth of the basis pontis
vignette: A 62-year-old hypertensive woman develops sudden clumsiness of her left hand and weakness of her left lower face, accompanied by dysarthria and hyperactive left deep tendon reflexes with a positive left Babinski sign. Testing of motor strength shows mild weakness (4/5) in the left arm, but finger tapping and rapid alternating movements in the left hand are severely slow, clumsy, and out of proportion to the motor weakness (dysarthria-clumsy hand syndrome). Sensation is completely intact.
question: Which anatomical structure is most classically infarcted in dysarthria-clumsy hand syndrome?
options: Posterior third of the posterior limb of the internal capsule
Ventral posterolateral (VPL) nucleus of the thalamus
Dentate nucleus of the ipsilateral cerebellum
Genu or anterior limb of the internal capsule, or the base of the rostral/middle pons
Primary motor cortex in the precentral gyrus

explanation.why_correct: Dysarthria-clumsy hand syndrome (one of Fisher's classical lacunar stroke syndromes) is characterized by severe dysarthria, facial weakness, dysphagia, and prominent clumsiness/dysmetria of the hand that is out of proportion to the mild motor weakness. It is caused by a small penetrating artery lacunar infarction located either in: (1) The genu / anterior limb of the internal capsule (and adjacent coronally descending fibers); or (2) The anterior upper to middle third of the basis pontis (disrupting crossing corticopontocerebellar fibers and corticobulbar fibers).
distractors: Posterior limb of the internal capsule infarction causes pure motor hemiparesis (proportional dense weakness of face, arm, and leg without prominent disproportionate cerebellar-like clumsiness).
VPL thalamic infarction causes pure sensory stroke.
The dentate nucleus causes true cerebellar intention tremor and limb dysmetria, but not upper motor neuron facial palsy and Babinski sign.
Cortical lesions typically cause associated cortical signs (aphasia, apraxia, neglect) not seen in lacunar syndromes.
explanation.key_point: Dysarthria-clumsy hand syndrome is a lacunar stroke localized to the genu/anterior limb of the internal capsule or the ventral basis pontis.

chapter: Vascular Syndromes of the Forebrain, Brainstem, and
source_quote: Bilateral border zone ischemia between the ACAs and MCAs results in bibrachial cortical sensorimotor impairment often confined to the forearms and hands
vignette: A 64-year-old man has a cardiac arrest during surgery with prolonged severe hypotension. On recovery he has bilateral arm weakness and sensory loss that is most evident in the forearms and hands, and he cannot make voluntary saccades on command.
question: Which border zone ischemia pattern best explains this presentation?
options: Bilateral border zone between the MCAs and PCAs
Border zone of all three major arterial systems (ACA, MCA, PCA)
Border zone between superficial and deep MCA territories on one side
Bilateral border zone between the ACAs and MCAs

explanation.why_correct: Bilateral border zone ischemia between the ACAs and MCAs causes bibrachial cortical sensorimotor impairment often confined to the forearms and hands, together with impaired volitional saccades.
distractors: Bilateral MCA-PCA border zone infarction causes cortical blindness, alexia, dyscalculia, dysgraphia and memory impairment, not bibrachial deficits.

Ischemia in the border zone of all three systems produces bilateral parieto-occipital infarcts with lower altitudinal field defects, difficulty judging size and distance, impaired smooth pursuit and optic ataxia.
A unilateral subcortical watershed infarct causes hemiparesis, often with hemisensory loss and aphasia or neglect, not bilateral arm deficits.
explanation.key_point: Bilateral ACA-MCA watershed infarcts give bibrachial sensorimotor deficits (forearms and hands) and impaired volitional saccades.

chapter: Vascular Syndromes of the Forebrain, Brainstem, and
source_quote: Bilateral border zone ischemia between the MCAs and PCAs results in cortical blindness, alexia, dyscalculia, dysgraphia, and memory impairment for verbal and nonverbal material
vignette: A 59-year-old woman has prolonged hypotension after cardiac surgery. She awakens unable to see, cannot read or calculate, has difficulty writing, and has trouble remembering both verbal and nonverbal material. Limb strength is not described as impaired.
question: Which pair of arterial territories shares the border zone most likely infarcted bilaterally?
options: ACA and MCA
MCA and PCA
PICA and AICA
Superficial and deep MCA branches

explanation.why_correct: Bilateral border zone ischemia between the MCAs and PCAs produces cortical blindness, alexia, dyscalculia, dysgraphia and memory impairment for verbal and nonverbal material.
distractors: ACA-MCA border zone infarcts cause bibrachial sensorimotor impairment and impaired volitional saccades, not cortical blindness and alexia.
The PICA, AICA and SCA border zones are in the cerebellum, not the cerebral cortex.
Superficial-deep MCA border zone (subcortical watershed) infarcts cause hemiparesis, hemisensory loss, and aphasia or neglect on one side.
explanation.key_point: Bilateral MCA-PCA watershed infarction: cortical blindness, alexia, dyscalculia, dysgraphia and memory loss.

chapter: Vascular Syndromes of the Forebrain, Brainstem, and
source_quote: A noncongruent homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing and a cortical type of hemihypesthesia (two-point discrimination, stereognosis) were common
vignette: A 72-year-old man with a known high-grade carotid stenosis has an episode of systemic hypotension. Afterward he has a noncongruent homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing and impaired two-point discrimination and stereognosis on the contralateral side. Limb strength is normal.
question: Which unilateral watershed zone was most likely infarcted?
options: Border zone between the superficial MCA and ACA territories
Border zone between the superficial and deep MCA territories
Border zone between the AChA and lenticulostriate territories
Border zone between the superficial MCA and PCA territories

explanation.why_correct: Posterior watershed infarcts between the superficial MCA and PCA territories commonly produce a noncongruent homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing and cortical-type hemihypesthesia (two-point discrimination, stereognosis); limb weakness is rare.
distractors: Anterior (MCA-ACA) watershed infarcts cause crural-predominant hemiparesis with facial sparing, with transcortical motor aphasia on the left.
Subcortical (superficial-deep MCA) watershed infarcts cause hemiparesis, often with hemisensory loss, and aphasia or neglect.
The AChA-lenticulostriate border is not a watershed pattern described for this syndrome in the chapter.
explanation.key_point: Posterior MCA-PCA watershed infarcts give noncongruent hemianopia with macular sparing and cortical sensory loss with little weakness.

chapter: Vascular Syndromes of the Forebrain, Brainstem, and
source_quote: results from bilateral damage to the basis pontis involving the rostral and midpontine segments interrupting descending corticobulbar and corticospinal pathways
vignette: A 60-year-old man has quadriplegia and cannot speak. He is awake and alert, follows commands by moving his eyes up and down and by blinking, but cannot move his eyes horizontally. His pupils react normally and his breathing is intact.
question: Which lesion best explains this picture?
options: Bilateral lesions of the pontine tegmentum involving the ascending reticular activating system
Bilateral medial medullary infarction
Bilateral damage to the basis pontis in the rostral and midpontine segments
Bilateral thalamic paramedian infarction

explanation.why_correct: Locked-in syndrome results from bilateral basis pontis damage that interrupts descending corticobulbar and corticospinal pathways. The ascending reticular activating system is spared, so wakefulness, vertical eye movements, blinking, pupillary reactivity and respiration are preserved.
distractors: Tegmental lesions involving the reticular activating system would impair wakefulness, which is preserved here.

Bilateral medial medullary infarction causes quadriplegia, medial lemniscal sensory loss, hypoglossal palsy, bulbar palsy and respiratory distress rather than preserved vertical eye movement with horizontal gaze loss.
Paramedian thalamic infarction causes hypersomnolence, memory loss, akinetic mutism and vertical gaze abnormalities rather than quadriplegia with preserved wakefulness.
explanation.key_point: Locked-in syndrome: bilateral ventral pons lesion with preserved wakefulness, vertical eye movements and blinking.

chapter: Vascular Syndromes of the Forebrain, Brainstem, and
source_quote: The lateral medullary syndrome (Wallenberg syndrome) often results from atherosclerotic steno-occlusive disease or dissection of the intracranial VA (V4) segment
vignette: A 58-year-old man has sudden vertigo, ipsilateral limb and gait ataxia, ipsilateral facial pain and temperature loss, hoarseness, dysphagia, and a right Horner syndrome. Pain and temperature sensation is lost on the left trunk and limbs. He has no limb weakness.
question: Which vessel lesion is the most frequent cause of this syndrome?
options: Atherosclerosis or dissection of the intracranial vertebral artery (V4 segment)
Occlusion of the anterior spinal artery
Occlusion of a paramedian branch of the basilar artery
Occlusion of the superior cerebellar artery

explanation.why_correct: The lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome often results from atherosclerotic steno-occlusive disease or dissection of the intracranial VA (V4) segment. Intrinsic PICA occlusion, small-vessel disease and cardiac embolism are other causes.
distractors: The anterior spinal artery supplies the medial medulla, causing tongue weakness and contralateral hemiparesis with loss of position and vibration sense.
Paramedian basilar branches produce the medial pontine syndromes (for example gaze paralysis, abducens palsy and contralateral hemiparesis).

SCA occlusion causes the lateral superior pontine and dorsal cerebellar syndromes with ipsilateral Horner syndrome, ataxia and contralateral hearing and pain-temperature loss; the nucleus ambiguus signs here point lower.
explanation.key_point: Wallenberg syndrome is most often due to intracranial vertebral artery (V4) disease or dissection, with PICA occlusion less common.

chapter: Vascular Syndromes of the Forebrain, Brainstem, and
source_quote: ipsilateral lower motor neuron weakness of half of the tongue and contralateral hemiparesis with associated loss of position sense and vibration
vignette: A 66-year-old man has atrophy and weakness of the right half of the tongue, with left hemiparesis sparing the face and loss of position sense and vibration on the left side. Pain and temperature sensation is normal.
question: Where is the infarct most likely located?
options: Lateral medulla
Medial medulla
Lateral inferior pons
Medial midbrain (cerebral peduncle)

explanation.why_correct: Medial medullary infarction involves the corticospinal tract rostral to its decussation, the hypoglossal fibers and nucleus, and the medial lemniscus, giving ipsilateral lower motor neuron tongue weakness and contralateral hemiparesis with loss of position and vibration sense, usually sparing the face.
distractors: Lateral medullary infarction causes ipsilateral facial pain and temperature loss, Horner syndrome and ataxia with contralateral pain and temperature loss, without limb weakness.
Lateral inferior pontine infarction (AICA) causes ipsilateral facial paralysis, deafness and ataxia with contralateral pain and temperature loss.
A medial midbrain lesion would produce an ipsilateral oculomotor palsy with contralateral hemiparesis, not tongue weakness.
explanation.key_point: Ipsilateral tongue weakness plus contralateral hemiparesis with lemniscal sensory loss and facial sparing localizes to the medial medulla.

chapter: Vascular Syndromes of the Forebrain, Brainstem, and
source_quote: Benedikt syndrome results from a lesion of the ventral mesencephalic tegmentum with involvement of the red nucleus, brachium conjunctivum, and CN III fascicles
vignette: A 63-year-old woman has a right oculomotor palsy with a dilated pupil. On the left side she has a new coarse tremor and choreoathetoid movements of the arm and leg. She has no hemiparesis.
question: Which midbrain structure is most likely involved along with the CN III fascicles?
options: Medial cerebral peduncle
Dorsal midbrain tectum
Medial aspect of the cerebral peduncle with horizontal gaze fibers
Red nucleus and brachium conjunctivum in the ventral tegmentum

explanation.why_correct: Benedikt syndrome results from a lesion of the ventral mesencephalic tegmentum involving the red nucleus, brachium conjunctivum and CN III fascicles. It causes ipsilateral CN III paresis, usually with pupillary dilation, and a contralateral hemitremor, hemiathetosis or hemichorea.
distractors: Medial cerebral peduncle involvement (Weber syndrome) damages corticospinal fibers and causes contralateral hemiparesis, which this patient lacks.
Dorsal midbrain lesions cause Parinaud syndrome with vertical gaze palsy, convergence-retraction nystagmus and light-near dissociation.
Interruption of horizontal gaze fibers in the medial cerebral peduncle (Foville) produces a contralateral conjugate gaze palsy, not tremor with a CN III palsy.
explanation.key_point: Ipsilateral CN III palsy with contralateral tremor, athetosis or chorea indicates a ventral tegmental lesion involving the red nucleus.

chapter: Vascular Syndromes of the Forebrain, Brainstem, and
source_quote: involving the medial cerebral peduncles, with subsequent damage to the CN III fascicles and corticospinal fibers
vignette: A 70-year-old man has a left oculomotor palsy with a dilated pupil and a right hemiparesis from corticospinal and corticobulbar tract involvement. There is no tremor or ataxia on the right.
question: Which structures are damaged in this infarct of penetrating PCA branches?
options: Medial cerebral peduncle with CN III fascicles and corticospinal fibers
Ventral tegmentum with red nucleus and brachium conjunctivum
Superior cerebellar peduncle in the midbrain
Dorsal midbrain and tectal plate

explanation.why_correct: Weber syndrome results from infarction in the territory of penetrating PCA branches involving the medial cerebral peduncles, with damage to the CN III fascicles and corticospinal fibers: ipsilateral oculomotor paresis with a dilated pupil and contralateral hemiparesis.
distractors: Ventral tegmental involvement with the red nucleus (Benedikt syndrome) adds contralateral hemitremor or chorea.
A superior cerebellar peduncle lesion (Nothnagel syndrome) combines ipsilateral CN III paresis with contralateral cerebellar ataxia rather than hemiparesis.
A dorsal midbrain lesion gives Parinaud syndrome with vertical gaze paralysis, not hemiparesis.
explanation.key_point: Weber syndrome: ipsilateral CN III palsy with dilated pupil plus contralateral hemiparesis from a medial peduncle lesion.

chapter: Vascular Syndromes of the Forebrain, Brainstem, and
source_quote: ipsilateral facial paralysis, impaired facial sensation, paralysis of conjugate gaze to the side of the lesion, deafness, tinnitus, and gait and limb ataxia
vignette: A 55-year-old woman has sudden right facial paralysis, decreased right facial sensation, right-sided deafness and tinnitus, right limb and gait ataxia, and loss of pain and temperature sensation on the left side of the body. Conjugate gaze to the right is paralyzed.
question: Occlusion of which artery most likely explains this lateral inferior pontine syndrome?
options: Posterior inferior cerebellar artery
Superior cerebellar artery
Anterior inferior cerebellar artery
Anterior spinal artery

explanation.why_correct: AICA territory strokes produce the lateral inferior pontine syndrome: ipsilateral facial paralysis, impaired facial sensation, paralysis of conjugate gaze toward the lesion, deafness, tinnitus and gait and limb ataxia, with contralateral hemibody loss of pain and temperature.
distractors: PICA occlusion is associated with the lateral medullary and inferior cerebellar syndromes, without facial paralysis and deafness.

SCA occlusion causes the lateral superior pontine syndrome (Horner syndrome, nystagmus, gaze paresis, hearing impairment, ataxia) without the ipsilateral facial paralysis and facial sensory loss listed for AICA.
Anterior spinal artery territory is the medial medulla, which causes tongue weakness and contralateral hemiparesis.
explanation.key_point: Ipsilateral facial palsy, deafness and tinnitus with ataxia and contralateral pain-temperature loss indicate AICA territory infarction.

chapter: Vascular Syndromes of the Forebrain, Brainstem, and
source_quote: Occlusion of the artery of Percheron results in bilateral paramedian thalamic infarctions with or without midbrain involvement
vignette: A 52-year-old man awakens with somnolence, then has memory loss and difficulty looking up. MRI shows symmetrical infarcts in both medial thalami with extension into the rostral midbrain, from occlusion of a single arterial trunk.
question: Which artery is most likely occluded?
options: Artery of Percheron
Thalamogeniculate arteries
Tuberothalamic (polar) artery
Posterior choroidal arteries

explanation.why_correct: The artery of Percheron is a single dominant trunk from a proximal PCA segment that supplies both paramedian thalami and the rostral midbrain; its occlusion causes bilateral paramedian thalamic infarcts with or without midbrain involvement.
distractors: Thalamogeniculate branches supply the posterolateral thalamus and cause pure sensory or sensorimotor stroke or thalamic pain.
The polar or tuberothalamic artery supplies the anterior thalamus, causing abulia, apathy, fluctuating alertness and personality change.
Posterior choroidal arteries supply the dorsal thalamus, causing quadrantanopia or sectoranopia and sensory loss of face and arm.
explanation.key_point: Artery of Percheron occlusion causes bilateral paramedian thalamic infarcts, with or without rostral midbrain involvement.

chapter: Vascular Syndromes of the Forebrain, Brainstem, and
source_quote: Occlusion of thalamogeniculate branches arising from the PCA (P2 segment) causes a pure sensory stroke, a sensorimotor stroke, or the thalamic pain syndrome
vignette: A 61-year-old man has sudden loss of all sensory modalities on the right side of the body, with sparing of the face. Months later he develops severe burning pain and allodynia in the affected limbs.
question: Occlusion of which arterial branches most likely caused the original infarct?
options: Paramedian thalamic-subthalamic arteries
Anterior choroidal artery
Thalamogeniculate branches of the PCA
Lateral lenticulostriate arteries of the MCA

explanation.why_correct: Occlusion of thalamogeniculate branches from the PCA (P2 segment) causes a pure sensory stroke, a sensorimotor stroke or the thalamic pain syndrome (Dejerine-Roussy); ventroposterolateral damage causes hemibody sensory loss with occasional facial sparing because of the more medial nucleus ventralis posteromedialis.
distractors: Paramedian branches cause hypersomnolence, memory loss, akinetic mutism and vertical gaze abnormalities rather than isolated hemisensory loss.
AChA infarction causes hemiparesis, hemianesthesia and homonymous hemianopia.
Lenticulostriate occlusion causes striatocapsular infarcts with hemiparesis and cortical-type signs rather than isolated pansensory loss and delayed thalamic pain.
explanation.key_point: Thalamogeniculate branch occlusion causes hemisensory loss (face may be spared) and may lead to delayed thalamic pain.

source_quote: vibration and position sense (medial lemniscal modalities) are often impaired on the paresthetic side, whereas sensation to pinprick and temperature (spinothalamic modalities) is preserved
vignette: A 67-year-old woman has numbness and paresthesias on the left side of the face, arm and leg. Examination shows impaired vibration and position sense on the left, but pinprick and temperature sensation are preserved. Ipsilateral smooth pursuit is impaired.
question: Where is the lacunar infarct most likely located?
options: Ventroposterolateral nucleus of the thalamus
Posterior limb of the internal capsule
Corona radiata
Paramedian dorsal pons

explanation.why_correct: In pontine pure sensory stroke, medial lemniscal modalities (vibration and position) are impaired while spinothalamic modalities (pinprick and temperature) are preserved, and ipsilateral smooth pursuit or VOR impairment may be present. Thalamic, capsular or corona radiata lesions affect both lemniscal and spinothalamic modalities.
distractors: A thalamic ventroposterolateral lacune typically compromises both spinothalamic and medial lemniscal modalities.
Internal capsule involvement also impairs both modality groups.
Corona radiata lesions impair both modality groups as well.
explanation.key_point: A dissociated loss (lemniscal impaired, spinothalamic preserved) in pure sensory stroke favors a pontine localization over thalamic or capsular sites.
